summary: Jon Postel's proposal for a person to hand out official socket numbers for standard protocols and publish where host-specific services can be found. He suggests ranges for network-wide standard functions, host-specific functions, reserved numbers and experiments. Initial assignments include Telnet, File Transfer, Remote Job Entry, Echo and Discard. It was replaced by RFC 433.

eli5.summary: Like a phone book for services. One person would give each service its own number, so everyone knows where to knock to reach file sharing or the echo service.

questions: how did port allocation work in the arpanet
subtitle: A proposal for centrally assigning and tracking network service port numbers.

tldr.problem: Different hosts used different port numbers for the same service, making it impossible for a client to know which port to use to reach, for example, the file transfer service.
tldr.mechanism: Jon Postel proposes that one person act as a 'czar' to hand out official port numbers for standard protocols, maintain a registry, and publish lists so everyone uses the same port for each service.
tldr.outcome: The idea was adopted and evolved into the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority), which still assigns port numbers and maintains registries for the Internet today.

today: RFC 433 replaced this with an updated registry, but the core idea of centralized number assignment persists. The IANA, founded on this principle, still assigns port numbers, IP address blocks, and protocol identifiers for the entire Internet.

sections.title: The Problem of Port Numbers
sections.content: The early ARPANET needed a way for client programs to find the server programs they wanted to talk to. Services like Telnet, File Transfer, and Echo each needed a port number. Without a central registry, different sites used different numbers, making network services impossible to find.
sections.eli5: Imagine if every town decided on its own what house number the library was at. You could not visit another town and find the library.

sections.title: Postel's Proposal
sections.content: Postel suggests that a single 'czar' maintain an official list of port numbers. The proposal divides the port space into ranges: sockets 0 to 63 for network-wide standard functions, 64 to 127 for host-specific services, 128 to 239 reserved for future use, and 240 to 255 for experimental use. Initial assignments include Telnet (socket 1), File Transfer (socket 3), and Echo (socket 7).
sections.eli5: Like a phone book where socket 1 always means 'Telnet', socket 3 always means 'file transfer', so everyone knows where to find each service.

sections.title: Lasting Impact
sections.content: This proposal was quickly adopted by the ARPANET community and evolved into the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA), which has grown to manage not only port numbers but also IP addresses, domain name extensions, protocol numbers, and many other critical Internet resources. The idea that a central authority should coordinate naming and numbering remains fundamental to the Internet.
sections.eli5: Postel's simple idea became the foundation for the system that still assigns addresses and numbers to keep the Internet running today.
